lead: Broadcasting copies one value from one processor to every other processor. Prefix sums, also called scan, give every element the running total of all elements up to and including it. (Some texts use the exclusive form, which leaves out the element itself and starts from x₀ = 0.) In this chapter y_i is the inclusive form. Both use a doubling idea: in broadcast the number of holders doubles each step; in scan the length of the summed block doubles from d to 2d each step. A broadcast finishes in ⌈log₂ p⌉ steps; a scan finishes in ⌈log₂ n⌉ steps. Scan appears in ranking, stream compaction, radix sort and load balancing. The simple scan is fast but does too much total work, so a two-level version restores work-optimality.
prereq: You need: tree and hypercube networks, parallel time and work, and log₂ notation from Unit 1, Foundations; 2.1 shows why data movement can set parallel cost.

blocks.text: Broadcast means one processor, called the root, holds a datum d and every one of the p processors needs a copy. On a tree network the root sends d to its children. Each child repeats the send to its own children. After one step two processors hold d, after two steps four hold it, and after k steps 2^k hold it. So every processor has d in ⌈log₂ p⌉ steps. The root may be any processor; the step count does not depend on which one.

On a hypercube the same doubling works dimension by dimension: at step k a holder sends along dimension k, and the number of holders doubles. All-to-all broadcast uses the same idea, but each processor starts with its own datum and every processor finishes with all p data; recursive doubling combines larger and larger groups. Broadcast carries a pivot, a block total or a termination signal, so it appears inside selection, sorting and graph algorithms.
Prefix sums, also called scan or all-prefix-sums, start with x₀, x₁, …, x_{n−1} and produce running totals. The last output y_{n−1} is the total of all inputs. A sequential loop uses n−1 additions.

blocks.where: y_i is the prefix sum at index i; x_j is the input at index j, for 0 ≤ j ≤ i.

blocks.text: The parallel doubling algorithm keeps a working array a, initially equal to x. At step d = 1, 2, 4, … every element with index i ≥ d sets a_i = a_i + a_{i−d}, using the values from before the step. For i ≥ d, after step d the value at i is the sum of the original block of length d+1 ending at i. After ⌈log₂ n⌉ steps every a_i is y_i. The parallel time is ⌈log₂ n⌉ steps.

blocks.where: W is the doubling scan's work in addition slots; n is the number of elements.

blocks.text: At step d, n−d elements do useful additions, but the simple cost count treats all n elements as active, giving n⌈log₂ n⌉ addition slots. That is Θ(n log₂ n) work, so the doubling scan is fast but not work-optimal. Every element must read old values, so use a barrier or a double buffer; otherwise an updated neighbour is read too early.

The two-level scan restores work-optimality. Split the n elements into p contiguous blocks of about n/p elements, one block per processor. Each processor scans its block sequentially and keeps the block total. Now the p block totals are prefix summed among the processors; doubling takes ⌈log₂ p⌉ steps. Each processor receives the sum of all block totals before its block, called its offset. It adds that offset to every element in its block. For p ≤ n this beats the simple doubling scan in work.

blocks.where: T_p is parallel time with p processors; n is the number of elements.

blocks.text: The total work is W = O(n + p log₂ p), which is O(n) when p is at most about n/log₂ n; alternatively one processor scans the p block totals sequentially in O(p) time, giving W = Θ(n) for p ≤ n. The two-level scan is the version used for ranking, stream compaction, counting, radix sort, quicksort partitioning and load balancing.

spec.aria: Four rows of eight cells: the input 3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6, then the array after adding values 1, 2 and 4 places to the left, ending 3 4 8 9 14 23 25 31.

examples.question: Take x = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] with n = 8, one element per processor. (a) Run the doubling prefix-sum algorithm and write the array after d = 1, d = 2 and d = 4. (b) Give the final prefix sums. (c) State the parallel time in steps. (d) Count the sequential additions, the doubling addition slots and the active additions; decide whether the doubling scan is work-optimal.
steps: Final prefix sums y = [3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25, 31]. Check: 3+1+4+1+5+9+2+6 = 31, the last cell.
Active additions in doubling: step d=1 has 7, d=2 has 6, d=4 has 4; total 17. Addition slots if all n elements are counted each step: 8×3 = 24.
Work is Θ(n log₂ n), not Θ(n), so the doubling scan is not work-optimal.
examples.answer: The final prefix sums are [3, 4, 8, 9, 14, 23, 25, 31]; parallel time is 3 steps, sequential work is 7 additions, doubling uses 24 addition slots or 17 active additions, so it is not work-optimal.
examples.check:
x = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
a = x[:]
d = 1
steps = 0
active = 0
while d < len(a):
    old = a[:]
    for i in range(d, len(a)):
        a[i] = old[i] + old[i - d]
        active += 1
    d *= 2
    steps += 1
for v in a:
    print(v)
print(steps)
print(len(x) - 1)
print(active)
print(steps * len(x))

traps: Updating in place and then reading new values: at step d every element must read the old value at i−d, so a barrier or a double buffer is needed.
Calling the doubling scan work-optimal: it uses n⌈log₂ n⌉ addition slots, which is Θ(n log₂ n), not O(n).
Swapping p and n: broadcast counts processors p, while prefix sums count elements n. The step counts are ⌈log₂ p⌉ and ⌈log₂ n⌉.
Reporting only the total: the prefix-sum output has n values, y₀ … y_{n−1}; the total is only y_{n−1}.
The favourite exam question asks for the array after every d, not only the final answer. Show each row and state which old values are added.

quiz.q: Define one-to-all broadcast and give its step count on p processors.
quiz.a: One root processor holds d and every processor receives a copy. On a tree or hypercube, each step doubles the number of holders, so it takes ⌈log₂ p⌉ steps.

quiz.q: Why does the doubling scan need a barrier or a double buffer?
quiz.a: At step d, element i must add the old value at i−d. If another processor has already overwritten that value in the same step, the result is wrong. A barrier or a second array keeps old values available.

quiz.q: For n = 16 elements, how many steps does the doubling scan take, and how many addition slots does it use?
With p = 10 processors on a tree, how many steps does one-to-all broadcast take?
quiz.a: ⌈log₂ 10⌉ = 4 steps, because 2³ = 8 holders is not enough and 2⁴ = 16 is enough.

quiz.q: Why is an O(n log n) scan not called work-optimal?
quiz.a: A sequential scan needs only n−1 additions, which is O(n) work. The doubling scan does Θ(n log n) work in total, so it uses more total operations than the best sequential method.

quiz.q: A two-level scan uses p = 1000 processors and n = 10⁶ elements. Give the block size and the parallel time order.
quiz.a: Block size = n/p = 10⁶/1000 = 1000 elements. Block totals are scanned in ⌈log₂ 1000⌉ ≈ 10 steps, so T_p ≈ n/p + log₂ p = 1000 + 10 = 1010 steps, i.e. T_p = O(n/p + log₂ p). The total work is O(n + p log₂ p), which is O(n) when p is at most about n/log₂ n.

quiz.q: Why can the two-level scan add block offsets to all elements of a block in one independent pass?
quiz.a: Every element in a block needs the same offset, the sum of all earlier block totals. Once that offset is known, each element's addition is independent of the others, so all elements of the block can be updated in parallel.

quiz.q: Name two uses of prefix sums in parallel computing.
quiz.a: Ranking elements and stream compaction; also counting, radix sort and load balancing.

beyond: Not for the exam. GPUs implement scan with Blelloch's up-sweep and down-sweep, and it is a core primitive in CUDA libraries. Stream compaction, sparse matrix assembly and database query execution use scan to turn a predicate into output positions. Many frameworks expose it as cumsum or exclusive_scan. Search next: parallel prefix sum, Blelloch scan, work-efficient scan, CUDA thrust inclusive_scan.
